title: Burnout
hook: Burnout looks like laziness from outside and feels like running on empty from inside, and the body usually shows it long before anyone says the word.
why:
Burnout is one of the most common ways that good workers fall apart, and one of the most misread. From outside, a burned-out colleague looks lazy, cynical, careless or disloyal. From inside, he feels drained, detached and useless, and often ashamed of feeling that way about work he used to care about. The people most at risk are often the most committed, which makes the misreading crueller.

This chapter teaches what burnout is and is not, how each of its three parts shows in the body and behaviour, why it is as much a problem of the job as of the person, how it overlaps with low mood, and what actually helps, for the person and for anyone who manages or works alongside him. Much of what follows applies beyond paid work, to carers and parents running on empty, but the research and the formal definitions concern work, and this chapter keeps to that.

teach.h: Burnout is a relationship with work that has gone wrong.
teach.p:
In 2019 the World Health Organization included burn-out in its International Classification of Diseases, but carefully. It is listed not as a medical condition but as an occupational phenomenon: a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. The classification describes three dimensions: feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion; increased mental distance from one's job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism about it; and reduced professional efficacy.

The definition draws on decades of research by Christina Maslach and colleagues, who have studied burnout since the 1970s, first among nurses, social workers and others in caring professions, and later across many kinds of work. The term itself was popularised in 1974 by the psychologist Herbert Freudenberger, who used it to describe the exhaustion and disillusionment he saw among dedicated volunteers at a free clinic, himself included.

Two points in the definition matter for a reader. First, burnout is about work. It is not the same as being tired, stressed or depressed in general, though it overlaps with all three. Second, it arises from chronic stress that has not been managed, which means the cause lies at least partly in the job: its demands, its resources, its fairness. Burnout is not simply a personal failure to cope.

When someone seems to have stopped caring about their work, the question to ask is not only *what is wrong with him?* but also *what has this job been asking of him, and for how long?*
teach.disconfirm: If burnout turned out to arise mainly from individual weakness, regardless of workload, control or fairness at work, the WHO's framing of it as an occupational phenomenon would be misleading. The research on work conditions described below suggests the job matters a great deal.
teach.pullQuote: Burnout is not simply a personal failure to cope.

teach.p:
The first and most visible dimension is exhaustion. It is not ordinary tiredness that a good night's sleep or a weekend fixes. It is a deep depletion that rest no longer touches. People describe waking up already tired, dreading Monday by Saturday afternoon, needing all their energy just to get through the day.

The body shows it. Movement slows. Posture slumps at the desk. Faces look grey and drawn. People catch every cold going and take longer to recover; the chapter on the stress posture described how chronic stress wears on the immune system and on sleep. Headaches, stomach problems and aching shoulders become regular. Many people sleep badly despite being exhausted, lying awake thinking about work or waking early with their mind already racing.

At work, exhaustion shows in behaviour over weeks: arriving later or leaving earlier, or the opposite, staying very late to keep up; more sick days; eating at the desk or not at all; snapping at small things; staring at the screen without seeming to take anything in.

None of these, alone, is burnout. Exhaustion can come from illness, a new baby, caring for a parent, poor sleep or a dozen other causes. What makes it suggestive of burnout is that it is tied to work, has lasted a long time, and comes with the other two dimensions described next.

Exhaustion also changes how a person reads others. The chapter on sleep and visible depletion later in this part describes how a tired brain sees more threat in faces. A depleted man may hear a colleague's neutral request as an attack, which feeds the irritability that others then notice. Some of what looks like his bad temper is simply the world as it looks through depletion.

Exhaustion that rest does not fix is a signal, not a character trait.
teach.disconfirm: If people's exhaustion in burnout lifted with an ordinary weekend's rest, as everyday tiredness does, it would not be the deep depletion described here. Most people who have been burned out describe rest that no longer restored them.

teach.p:
The second dimension is mental distance from the job, often showing as cynicism. People who once cared deeply begin to protect themselves by caring less. They make sarcastic remarks about the organisation, the customers or the patients. They say *it's just a job* about work that used to matter to them. In caring professions, Maslach called this depersonalisation: treating patients, pupils or clients as cases or numbers rather than people.

It shows in the body as withdrawal. The face becomes flatter and less animated in meetings. Eye contact shortens. People stop joining in: eating alone, skipping social events, turning their camera off on video calls, contributing the minimum. Some become irritable and dismissive; others go quiet and compliant, doing what is asked and nothing more.

This is the dimension most often misread, because it looks so much like a bad attitude. Managers respond to cynicism with discipline, and colleagues respond to withdrawal by withdrawing in turn. Both make it worse. The distance is, in most cases, a defence: a person protecting what is left of himself from a job that has taken more than he can give.

For a reader, the useful comparison is with the person's own past. Was this man always sardonic and detached, or has he become so? A cynic who used to be an idealist is often a burned-out idealist.

Notice too who is not being asked. In many workplaces, a man who has gone quiet and sardonic is assumed to be tough or simply unbothered. The colleague who has stopped joking at lunch, who sighs at every new request, whose emails have shrunk to a single line, may be saying more through those changes than he would ever say in words.

Cynicism in a once-committed person is often care that has run out of fuel.
teach.disconfirm: If the colleagues who became cynical and withdrawn at work had always been that way, rather than changing over time, distance would be a matter of temperament rather than burnout. The change from baseline is what matters.

teach.h: Efficacy: 'I'm no good at this any more.'
teach.p:
The third dimension is a reduced sense of professional efficacy: feeling incompetent, unproductive, unable to make a difference. People who were good at their jobs start to doubt that they ever were. Tasks that used to take an hour take a day. Decisions get put off. Mistakes creep in, and each one feeds the sense of failing.

From outside, this can look like declining performance, and it often is. But the decline is usually a consequence of exhaustion and distance rather than a sign that the person has stopped trying. Many burned-out people are trying harder than ever and getting less done, which is one of the most demoralising experiences there is.

Watch for compensation as well. Some people respond to falling efficacy by working longer and longer hours, which deepens the exhaustion and leaves even less energy for doing the work well. In a burned-out person, very long hours are often a symptom rather than a solution, and praising them can make things worse.

The body shows effort without result. Long hours at the desk with little to show. The head in the hands over a task that should be simple. A furrowed brow and a slump when someone asks how a project is going. Self-criticism in conversation, often disguised as humour: *I'm useless, me.*

This dimension carries a particular risk for men whose sense of themselves is closely tied to competence at work. When the work goes, or seems to go, it can feel like losing who they are, and the chapter on the I'm Fine mask described how men in that position often hide it.

When a capable man starts calling himself useless, take it seriously, and do not simply argue him out of it.
teach.disconfirm: If people whose sense of efficacy collapsed under burnout were generally less capable than their colleagues to begin with, this dimension would be about ability rather than burnout. Burnout often strikes the most committed and capable, which is why the change matters more than the level.

teach.h: It is about the job as well as the person.
teach.p:
Maslach and her colleague Michael Leiter describe burnout as the result of a mismatch between a person and their job, in one or more of six areas of work life. Workload: too much to do, with too few resources. Control: too little say over how the work is done. Reward: good work that goes unrecognised. Community: a team marked by incivility, conflict or isolation rather than support. Fairness: decisions that feel unjust or discriminatory. Values: being asked to do things that conflict with what the person believes is right.

This framework has a practical consequence that is easy to miss. If burnout comes from mismatches in the job, then solutions aimed only at the person, such as resilience workshops, mindfulness apps and wellness weeks, will often miss the point. They may help a little, but they leave the mismatch in place, and can send the message that the problem lies in the worker's inability to cope with an unreasonable situation.

For a reader who manages people, this means that when you see the signs of burnout in someone on your team, the most useful questions are about the six areas. What is his workload compared with six months ago? How much control does he have? Is his work recognised? How is the team treating him? Has anything felt unfair? Is he being asked to do things that sit badly with him?

And ask, rather than decide. Maslach and Leiter advise leaders to involve people in identifying and fixing the mismatch rather than imposing their own solutions.

When burnout spreads through a team, look at the team's conditions before you look at its members.
teach.disconfirm: If people's burnout improved just as much from personal resilience training as from changes to workload, control, fairness and recognition, the mismatch model would be wrong. The research Maslach and Leiter draw on suggests the job conditions matter a great deal.

teach.p:
Burnout and depression share a great deal: exhaustion, withdrawal, poor sleep, feelings of uselessness. Researchers continue to debate how far they are the same thing seen from different angles, and some studies find substantial overlap. What matters for a reader is not the label but the reach of the difficulty.

Burnout, in the WHO's definition, is about work. If a man's exhaustion, detachment and sense of failure extend well beyond work, if he has stopped enjoying his family, his friends and his hobbies, if he feels hopeless about life in general, if his sleep has collapsed, then what he is experiencing may be more than burnout, and the chapter on depression's physical signature applies. That is not a reason to argue with him about which word fits. It is a reason to encourage him to see a doctor, who can help tell these apart and look for physical causes too.

It is also a reason to listen carefully for hopelessness. Men who have lost their sense of themselves through work, through burnout, redundancy or failure, are at raised risk of suicide. If you hear talk of being a burden, of there being no way out, or of not wanting to go on, ask directly whether he is thinking about ending his life. The chapter on suicidal ideation explains how, and the crisis resources are one tap away.

Burnout is a word for what work has done. It is not a ceiling on how serious things can get.
teach.disconfirm: If burnout and low mood never overlapped, with burned-out workers always well outside work, there would be no need to look beyond the job. The overlap researchers report is a reason to ask about life beyond work too.

teach.p:
For the person himself, the research on recovery from work points first to rest that is actually rest. Sabine Sonnentag and colleagues have found that psychologically detaching from work during time off, not checking email, not rehearsing problems, being absorbed in something else, is linked to better wellbeing and less exhaustion. Physical activity, time with people who matter, and sleep all help. So do boundaries: a time when work stops, a phone that goes in a drawer.

But recovery cannot outrun a mismatch that continues. The person also needs to name the problem with someone who can change it: a manager, a union representative, human resources. Talking to a doctor is worthwhile too, both for the sleep and health effects and to check whether something more than burnout is going on. Some people need time off; some need a change of role or job.

For colleagues and managers, the most useful responses follow from the earlier blocks. Notice changes from the person's baseline. Ask, privately and without judgment, how he is and what has changed at work. Ask specifically about load, control, recognition, fairness and support. Then change what you can, and say what you cannot. Recognise good work out loud. Protect time off. Do not send a burned-out man to a resilience workshop and leave his workload as it was.

And notice your own. Burnout is easier to see in others than in yourself, because it erodes the very energy and judgment you would need to notice it. The chapter on building an early-warning system at the end of this part asks you to decide, now, what your first signs would be.
teach.disconfirm: If people recovering from burnout did just as well while continuing to check work email in the evenings and with their workload unchanged, the advice to detach and fix the mismatch would be unnecessary. The research on recovery suggests otherwise.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seeing a change from who he was, and asking what changed at work.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading a once-keen colleague's cynicism as a bad attitude.
poseGallery.annotation: Cynicism in a once-committed person is often a defence against a job that has taken too much.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking about his workload, control and support.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sending him on a resilience course.

poseGallery.annotation: Errors from a once-careful worker often follow exhaustion and distance. Asking about the job comes before managing the person.

caseStudy:
Ravi, thirty-eight, teaches maths at a busy secondary school and has a reputation as one of its best teachers. For years he ran the chess club at lunchtime and stayed late to help pupils before exams. In the autumn, Graham, his head of department, notices changes. Ravi has stopped running the chess club. In the staffroom he makes sour jokes about the pupils being just numbers on a spreadsheet. He looks grey, has been off sick three times since September, and twice has forgotten to set cover work.

Another senior teacher suggests a quiet word about professionalism. Graham decides to ask a different question first. He catches Ravi at the end of a day, sits with him in an empty classroom, and says that Ravi seems shattered and not himself, and asks what has changed this term. Ravi says he is fine. Graham waits. Then Ravi says that since two colleagues left in the summer and were not replaced, he has been teaching an extra five lessons a week, covering another teacher's exam classes, and marking until midnight. He feels he is failing every class he teaches.

Graham takes the workload to the head the next day, with the numbers. Two of Ravi's extra classes are moved to a supply teacher. Graham also tells Ravi, plainly, that his teaching is still among the best in the department, and suggests he see his doctor about his sleep. Ravi does, and his doctor also asks about his mood more broadly; it is mainly work, Ravi says, and the doctor agrees to see him again in a month.

Ravi starts leaving his marking at school on Fridays. By February he is less grey. In March, a pupil asks whether chess club is coming back. Ravi says it might, on Thursdays.
observe: Notice whether anyone at your work has changed over recent months from committed to cynical, from present to withdrawn, from capable to self-doubting.
Notice how your organisation responds to signs of burnout: with changes to the work, or with programmes aimed at the person.
Notice how often you check work messages in your own time, and how you feel afterwards.

drills.name: Three Dimensions
steps: Think of someone at work who seems to be struggling.
Write what you have seen under each heading: exhaustion, distance or cynicism, and reduced efficacy.
For each, note how it compares with how they were a year ago.
Note anything that suggests the difficulty reaches beyond work.
Write one private, behaviour-first question you could ask them.
variations: Do the exercise for yourself, honestly, and compare the picture with how you were a year ago.
Do the exercise for someone outside work, such as a carer or a parent at home, and see which dimensions apply.

drills.name: Six Areas Check
steps: Choose your own job or the job of someone you manage.
Rate each of the six areas from one to five: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values.
Mark the two weakest areas.
For each, write one change that would help, and who could make it.
Write one sentence you could use to raise it with that person.
variations: Ask a colleague to rate the six areas for their own job, and compare their weakest areas with yours.
Rate the six areas for a job you left, and see whether the weakest areas explain why you left.

drills.name: Detachment Week
steps: Choose a time each evening after which you will not read or think about work.
Put your work phone or notifications away at that time for a week.
Fill the time with something absorbing, such as exercise, a hobby or people.
Each night, note how often your mind went back to work and what you did about it.
At the end of the week, compare your energy with the week before.
variations: Extend the detachment to one whole weekend day, and note what you did with the time.
Ask someone you live with to tell you when they notice you thinking or talking about work after your chosen time.

drills.name: Recognition Habit
steps: Think of three people whose good work you have noticed recently and not mentioned.
Write one specific sentence of recognition for each.
Say or send each sentence this week.
Notice their response.
Write down how often you usually give recognition, honestly.
variations: Give recognition to someone more senior than you, such as your manager, and notice their response.
Recognise someone's effort on a piece of work that went badly, not only on what went well.

drills.name: Your First Signs
steps: Think back to the most depleted period of your working life.
Write down the first signs that appeared in your body, behaviour and attitude.
Write which of the six areas was most out of balance at the time.
Write who noticed, if anyone, and what they did.
Write one thing you would do differently if those first signs appeared again.
variations: Share your first signs with one person at work and one at home, and ask them to tell you if they see them.
Write down which of the six areas you would most want to protect in your next job, and why.

quiz.q: A once-keen colleague has become sarcastic, withdrawn and error-prone over several months. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That he has a bad attitude and needs a formal warning to refocus him
That he is lazy and has stopped caring about the people he works with
That these may be signs of burnout; ask about his load and what has changed
That he is depressed and should be sent home until he has recovered
quiz.explain: Exhaustion, cynicism and falling efficacy together, as a change from his baseline, fit burnout, which arises partly from the job. A private question about workload, control and support is more useful than discipline or a diagnosis.

quiz.q: How does the World Health Organization's ICD-11 classify burn-out?
options: As an occupational phenomenon from chronic workplace stress, not a medical condition
As a serious mental illness that requires treatment with medication
As a personality trait found mainly in people who dislike hard work
As a general term for feeling tired in any area of life, not only work
quiz.explain: The WHO describes burn-out as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It says the term should be applied only to experiences at work, not to other areas of life.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of Maslach and Leiter's six areas of work life linked to burnout?
options: The length of a person's daily commute
The temperature of the office
The size of a person's salary alone
Fairness
quiz.explain: The six areas are workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Mismatches between person and job in these areas drive burnout, so they are where to look for solutions.

quiz.q: Your team's best engineer seems exhausted and cynical. Human resources suggests sending him on a resilience workshop. What fits this chapter?
options: Send him on the workshop, since resilience is what he is lacking
Ask him about workload, control and support, and change what you can
Tell him to take a week's holiday and come back when he feels better
Wait to see whether his performance falls before doing anything at all
quiz.explain: Burnout arises from mismatches in the job, so changes to workload, control, recognition and fairness matter most. A workshop alone leaves the mismatch in place and can imply the problem is his.

quiz.q: What are the three dimensions of burn-out in the WHO definition?
options: Anger, anxiety and low mood, at work and at home
Overwork, underpayment and poor management by others
Exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, and reduced efficacy
Insomnia, weight loss and frequent illness over several months
quiz.explain: Energy depletion, increased mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy. Each shows in the body and behaviour, and each is often misread as a character flaw.

quiz.q: A friend says work has burned him out, and also that he has stopped enjoying anything outside work, sleeps badly and feels hopeless. What fits this chapter?
options: Encourage him to see a doctor, as this may be more than burnout, and ask how he is
Tell him that burnout always passes once a person has a good long holiday
Advise him to resign immediately, since the job is clearly the whole problem
Suggest a mindfulness app, which should be enough to help him recover
quiz.explain: When exhaustion and hopelessness reach well beyond work, it may be more than burnout. Encouraging a doctor helps tell these apart, and hopelessness is a reason to ask directly whether he has had thoughts of suicide.

quiz.q: Who popularised the term burnout in 1974, and among which group?
options: Herbert Freudenberger, describing volunteers at a free clinic
Christina Maslach, describing professional footballers at the end of their careers
The World Health Organization, describing factory workers in several countries
Sigmund Freud, describing his own patients during the early years of psychoanalysis
quiz.explain: Herbert Freudenberger used the term in 1974 to describe the exhaustion and disillusionment he saw among dedicated volunteers at a free clinic, himself included. Maslach's research came later and gave it its three dimensions.

quiz.q: A nurse who used to know every patient by name now refers to them by bed number, looks grey and eats alone. Her matron wants a formal talk about attitude. What fits this chapter best?
options: Hold the formal talk at once, since referring to patients by number is unprofessional
Send her on an online resilience course and review her attitude again in six months
Ask her privately how things have been, and look at her workload and support
Move her to another ward without explanation, so that the problem goes away
quiz.explain: Bed numbers, a grey face and withdrawal fit the distance and exhaustion of burnout, and a change from a caring baseline points to the conditions. Asking, and changing the workload, does more than a talk about attitude.

quiz.q: Someone says that a good two-week holiday will cure anyone's burnout. What does the research suggest?
options: It is right, since a fortnight away resets the body's stress systems completely
The benefits usually fade within weeks of return if the work stays the same
It is right, but only if the holiday is spent somewhere with a hot climate
It is wrong, since holidays make burnout worse by adding travel stress
quiz.explain: Studies reviewed by de Bloom and colleagues found that holiday benefits tend to fade within a few weeks of returning to work. Without changes to the work itself, burnout tends to come back.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific period when you, or someone close to you, came near to burning out. Describe what showed in the body and behaviour under each of the three dimensions: exhaustion, distance, and reduced efficacy. Which of the six areas of work life was most out of balance? What did people around you do, and what would have helped more? If the same signs appeared in a colleague tomorrow, what is the first question you would ask?
reflection.guidance: Many men recognise burnout in themselves only in hindsight, because it erodes the energy and judgment needed to notice it. Be specific about the six areas: naming the mismatch, such as workload or fairness, points to what could change. The question you write at the end should be private, behaviour-first, and about the work as well as the person.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read burnout as a character flaw, treating the exhausted, cynical, error-prone colleague as lazy, disloyal or incompetent, and responding with discipline. The second is to treat it as entirely the person's problem, offering resilience courses and wellness apps while the workload, unfairness or lack of control continue. The third is to miss the change from baseline, judging someone as they are now rather than as they were. The fourth is to stop at the word burnout when the difficulty reaches well beyond work and may need a doctor. And the quietest failure is to miss it in yourself, because burnout erodes the very capacity you would need to notice it. Ask about the job as well as the person, change what can be changed, and keep an eye on your own first signs.

moreCases.title: The nurse who started saying 'bed six'
moreCases.scene:
Joy, forty-one, has been a nurse on a busy surgical ward for twelve years. She is the one the students ask for, the one relatives remember by name. Over the past year the ward has lost four nurses and replaced two, and Joy has been working extra shifts most weeks. Her ward manager, Sandra, has started to notice changes. Joy no longer chats with patients as she does her rounds. At handover she refers to them by bed number: "bed six is post-op, bed nine needs a scan." Her face is flat and grey, and she has stopped joining the others in the staff room, eating at the nurses' station instead, staring at her phone. Last week a relative complained that Joy had been curt with her mother.

The matron suggests a formal conversation about attitude, and says that the trust offers an online resilience course that Joy could be asked to complete.

Sandra is not sure. She has worked beside Joy for eight years, and the woman at the nurses' station does not look like someone with a bad attitude. She looks like someone who has been emptied out.

Sandra has also noticed that Joy has stopped bringing in the homemade cakes she used to bring every Friday, and that she no longer stays to chat at the end of a shift. Last month she forgot her own birthday until a student mentioned it.

Joy's husband rang the ward once, last month, to ask whether she had been held up at work. She had left on time. She had been sitting in her car in the hospital car park for an hour before she could face driving home.
moreCases.misread:
The matron read Joy's flatness, curtness and bed numbers as an attitude problem, something to be corrected through a formal conversation and a course. That reading placed the whole difficulty inside Joy, and none of it in the ward.

And because the trust's response to burnout was a course, it also sent Joy a message: that the problem was her ability to cope, not the number of nurses on the ward.

The relative's complaint also became, in the matron's eyes, proof of a pattern, when a single curt exchange from an exhausted nurse after a fourteen-hour shift says more about the shift than about the nurse.
moreCases.betterRead:
Joy showed all three of the WHO's dimensions of burn-out: exhaustion in her grey face and her eating alone; distance in the bed numbers, which Maslach called depersonalisation, a way of protecting oneself by caring less; and, in the complaint, the beginning of reduced efficacy. Against twelve years of baseline as the ward's most caring nurse, the change pointed less to her character than to her conditions. Maslach and Leiter's six areas fitted closely: workload far too high, little control over shifts, care unrecognised, and a team stretched thin. A resilience course would have treated the symptom and left the cause. Sandra's better approach was to ask Joy, privately, how the past year had been, and to listen. Joy cried, and said she no longer recognised herself. Sandra stopped asking her to cover extra shifts, protected her days off, told the matron that the ward needed more staff rather than more courses, and made sure Joy's work was thanked, out loud, at the next team meeting.

Joy said later that what helped most was not the days off but being asked. Nobody had asked her how she was for over a year.

moreCases.title: The owner who could not switch off
moreCases.scene:
Callum, forty-five, runs a small building firm he started fifteen years ago. He has eight employees and a reputation for doing things properly. This year has been brutal: a supplier went bust, two clients have not paid, and he has been working seven days a week to keep the business going. His wife, Leanne, watches him change. He falls asleep on the sofa at half past eight and wakes at four, unable to get back to sleep. He checks his phone constantly, including at the dinner table. He has stopped going to his son's football matches. When Leanne asks how the business is, he says, "What's the point? Every time I fix something, something else breaks."

Leanne suggests a holiday. Callum says he cannot possibly take one, and then, when she books a week in Spain anyway, he spends most of it on his phone by the pool. Two days after they get back, he looks exactly as he did before they left.

His brother, who also runs a business, tells Leanne that Callum just needs to toughen up, because that is what running a firm is like.

Callum has also started drinking more in the evenings, two or three beers where he used to have one, and has stopped going to the gym he went to every morning for ten years. He says he does not have time.

Callum's employees have noticed too. His foreman says he snaps at them over small mistakes and then apologises, which he never used to do, and that he has started doing jobs himself rather than trusting anyone else to do them.
moreCases.misread:
His brother read Callum's exhaustion and pessimism as a lack of toughness. Leanne's own first reading, that a break would fix it, treated a long-running mismatch with his work as ordinary tiredness that rest could cure.

His own reading was the cruellest. He took his exhaustion as proof that he was failing his business, his family and his employees, which pushed him to work harder still.

The holiday reading was kind and understandable. It simply treated the symptom, tiredness, as the cause, and so promised a cure that a week could not deliver.
moreCases.betterRead:
Burnout is not confined to employees, and owners of small businesses often have the heaviest workload and the least chance to switch off. Callum's exhaustion that sleep did not fix, his cynical "what's the point?" and his sense that nothing he did made a difference fit all three dimensions. A holiday spent on the phone gave him no psychological detachment from work, which Sonnentag's research links to recovery, and the pressures were waiting when he got back. Leanne's better approach, after the holiday, was to talk with Callum about the work itself rather than his attitude to it. They looked at what was making it unmanageable. He agreed to ask his accountant about chasing the unpaid invoices, to give his foreman more responsibility, and to keep Sundays work-free, with the phone switched off. He also agreed to see his doctor about his sleep. It took months. The first sign of change was that he came to a football match and did not look at his phone once.

He also told his foreman, for the first time, that he was struggling. The foreman said he had noticed months ago and had been waiting to be asked to help.

moreCases.title: The agent who read from the script
moreCases.scene:
Tariq, thirty-two, has worked in a bank's customer complaints team for six years. He used to be its best agent: warm, patient, good at calming angry callers. Since a reorganisation last year, the team has been given strict targets for call length and must follow a script, with calls monitored and scored. Tariq's manager, Fiona, has noticed that he now reads the script word for word, in a flat voice. His calls are short, but his customer satisfaction scores have fallen. He sighs before every call, rubs his eyes often, and sits slumped with his headset half off between calls. He has taken more sick days this year than in the previous five combined.

Fiona's own manager sees the falling scores and tells her to put Tariq on a performance improvement plan.

Fiona has been in the team for as long as Tariq. She remembers that he once spent forty minutes on the phone with an elderly man whose savings had been stolen, and got a letter of thanks from the man's daughter.

Tariq has also stopped joining the team's quiz on Friday afternoons, which he used to organise. When a new agent asks him for advice, he says, "Just stick to the script, mate. It's easier."

Fiona has also noticed that Tariq no longer eats his lunch in the break room with the others. He takes it outside and sits on the low wall by the car park, alone, with his headphones in, even when it is raining. When she asked him last week how he was, he said, "Living the dream," and laughed, without smiling.
moreCases.misread:
Fiona's manager read Tariq's falling scores and flat delivery as declining performance to be managed. He did not ask why one of the best agents in the team had started to perform like one of the worst.

It also treated the scores as the whole truth, when the scores were measuring the very targets that had changed how Tariq was allowed to work.

And the performance plan would have tested Tariq against the very targets that had caused the problem, which is a reliable way to make a good employee leave.
moreCases.betterRead:
Maslach and Leiter's six areas explain much of what had happened to Tariq. The reorganisation had taken away his control over how he did the work, set targets that rewarded short calls rather than good ones, and clashed with his values, which were about helping people properly. His flat voice and word-for-word script were distance: the shutters coming down to protect someone who could no longer do the job the way he believed it should be done. His slump, his sighs and his sick days were exhaustion. A performance plan would have added pressure to a mismatch that the job itself had created. Fiona's better approach was to ask Tariq what had changed for him, and then to take what he said to her own manager. She argued for agents being allowed to go off script and spend longer on complex complaints. The bank agreed to trial it for experienced agents. Tariq's satisfaction scores rose within a month, and he told Fiona it felt like being allowed to do his job again.

He also started training new agents again, which gave him back the part of the job he had always loved.

moreCases.title: The father at the end of his rope
moreCases.scene:
Dev, thirty-nine, gave up his job as a graphic designer two years ago to stay at home with his twins, now three, while his wife, Priya, returned to her career as a solicitor. He loves his children. But by the second winter, he is running on empty. He is short with the twins and then guilty about it. He has stopped meeting his friends, stopped drawing, and spends nap times staring at the wall rather than resting. When Priya comes home, he hands the children over and goes upstairs without a word. He tells her, one night, that he feels like he is failing at the only thing he is supposed to be doing, and that he does not feel anything for the twins some days, which frightens him.

Priya's mother tells her that looking after children is what parents have always done, and that Dev should be grateful he does not have to go out to work.

Priya has read about burnout at work and wonders whether something similar can happen at home.

Dev has also stopped looking after himself. He eats the twins' leftovers instead of meals, has not had a haircut in months, and wears the same tracksuit most days. When a friend from his old job messaged him, he did not reply for three weeks.

Priya has also noticed that Dev flinches when the twins cry at night, and lies rigid in bed waiting for the next cry. He used to sleep through anything.
moreCases.misread:
Priya's mother read Dev's exhaustion and detachment as ingratitude, because caring for children is supposed to be natural and rewarding, and because the work of a parent at home is rarely seen as work at all.

And Dev's own reading, that he was failing as a father, was the kind of judgment that burnout feeds on and that keeps people from asking for help.

It also missed that Dev had no colleagues, no breaks and no end to his working day, which in any other job would be called unreasonable.
moreCases.betterRead:
The WHO's definition of burn-out is about paid work, but researchers such as Isabelle Roskam and Moïra Mikolajczak have studied a similar pattern in parents: overwhelming exhaustion, emotional distance from the children, and a sense of no longer being the parent one wants to be. Dev's cluster fitted that pattern, and his feeling of nothing for his children some days was a reason to take it seriously rather than a reason for shame. Several of Maslach and Leiter's areas apply at home as much as at work: a relentless workload, little control over the day, little recognition and few adults to talk to. Priya's better response was to treat it as a problem of load, not of love. They found a nursery for two mornings a week, Priya took over bedtimes three nights a week, and Dev started meeting another stay-at-home father on Fridays. Because his low feelings reached so far, and frightened him, Priya also encouraged him to see their doctor, and went with him.

Dev also started drawing again, at nap times, which he said made him feel like himself for an hour a day.

workedReading.title: The one-to-one after the merger
workedReading.scene:
Leanne manages a finance team that was merged with another department six months ago. One of her team, Phil, fifty-four, has been there for twenty years and knows more about the old systems than anyone. Since the merger, Leanne has noticed that Phil arrives just on time and leaves exactly on time, which he never used to do. In meetings he sits back with his arms folded and says, "Whatever you think," to most suggestions. His reports, once immaculate, have contained three errors this quarter. He looks tired all the time, and twice she has seen him sitting in his car in the car park for twenty minutes before coming in. A colleague from the merged department has described him as "dead wood".

Leanne also knows that the merger has been hard on everyone, including herself, and that she has had less time for her team than usual. She wonders whether she has contributed to whatever is happening to Phil.

She also knows that people in the merged department see the old team as resistant to change, and that Phil has become a symbol of that in their eyes. Whatever she does will be watched by both sides.

steps.label: Sort what you see
steps.text:
Leanne sorts her observations under the three dimensions. Exhaustion: looking tired all the time, sitting in his car before coming in. Distance: arms folded, "whatever you think", leaving on the dot. Efficacy: errors in reports that used to be perfect. All three are present, and all three are changes since the merger.

She also notes that the dimensions appeared in order: tiredness first, in the first month after the merger, then the distance, then the errors. That order is common, and it suggests the problem has been building for some time.

Sorting her observations also helps her avoid leading with the errors. The errors are the part that would go in a performance file. The exhaustion and distance are the part that would explain them.

steps.label: Compare with his baseline
steps.text:
For twenty years, Phil was the person who stayed late at year end, who trained every new starter and who argued, sometimes stubbornly, for doing things properly. "Whatever you think" is the opposite of the man she knew. The size of the change makes it unlikely that he has simply become lazy, and the timing points to something about the merger.

She also notes the things that have not changed. He is still polite, still punctual, still reliable in the basics. The core of the man is there; it is the extra effort, the care beyond the job description, that has gone.

She also remembers a conversation from years ago, when Phil told her that the best part of his job was being the person everyone came to with problems. Since the merger, nobody comes to him.

steps.label: Check the six areas
steps.text:
She thinks through the six areas of work life. Workload has risen: he is now supporting two systems. Control has fallen: decisions about processes are made by the merged department's managers. Reward: his expertise in the old systems is now treated as obsolete. Community: the new colleagues talk about him rather than to him. Fairness and values may also be in play. Several areas are badly out of balance.

She also notices that her own part in the six areas is real. She has not recognised his work since the merger, and she has not argued for his views in the new management meetings. Some of the mismatch is in her gift to change.

She also asks herself which of the six areas she could change this month, and which would need someone more senior. Recognition and his role in the migration are hers to give. The workload across two systems is not, and she will have to argue for it.

steps.label: Hold the readings open
steps.text:
Leanne notes that burnout is one possibility, and that there are others: a health problem, something at home, low mood that reaches beyond work, or a mixture. She does not need to decide which. She decides to ask, privately, without mentioning the errors first, and to listen for whether the difficulty seems to be about work or about more than work.

She also considers whether he might be preparing to leave or retire. If so, that would be his choice to make, and a frank conversation would help him make it well.

She also decides that if he tells her the problem is mainly outside work, she will listen, offer support through the employee assistance line and flexibility, and encourage him to see his doctor, rather than trying to fix it herself.

steps.label: Ask about the work
steps.text:
In a one-to-one, she says, "Phil, you've been here longer than anyone, and this merger has changed a lot. How has it been for you, honestly?" He is silent for a long moment, then says that he feels like a dinosaur, that nobody asks his opinion any more, that he is doing two jobs and that he cannot see the point of trying to do either properly when the new managers will change it all again.

She also lets the silence sit before he answers. A man who feels unheard will often test whether a question is real by waiting to see whether the person asking will fill the gap.

She also does not argue with his sense of being a dinosaur, or tell him he is wrong to feel it. She says that she can see why he feels that way, given how the merger has gone.

steps.label: Make a change together
steps.text:
Leanne thanks him for being straight with her. She asks what would help most, and he says having a say. She asks him to lead the migration of the old system's reports, using exactly the knowledge the others have dismissed, and moves one of his routine tasks to a new colleague. She also tells the merged department's manager, firmly, that Phil's expertise is essential. She asks Phil how he is outside work, and he says fine, his garden is keeping him sane, which tells her the difficulty seems mostly to sit at work.

She also asks him how he would like her to raise his concerns with the new managers, so that he keeps some control over how his views are presented.

She also sets a date to review it with him in six weeks, so that the change is not a one-off gesture but something they will both come back to.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Over the next two months, Phil's arms unfold in meetings. He starts arguing again, stubbornly, for doing things properly, which Leanne finds she has missed. The errors stop. He still leaves on time, which she decides is no bad thing. She notes that the colleague who called him dead wood now asks him for help with the old reports most weeks, and that a disciplinary conversation would have cost the team its most knowledgeable member.

She also changes her own habits. She now spends ten minutes each week with each member of the team asking how the work is going, rather than waiting for problems to show up in the reports.

She also mentions to her own manager what she has learned, without naming Phil, because she suspects that others from the old department are struggling in the same way.

moreFailures.title: Reading burnout as laziness or a bad attitude
moreFailures.body:
From outside, burnout looks like a series of character flaws: tiredness that looks like laziness, cynicism that looks like disloyalty, mistakes that look like carelessness, withdrawal that looks like not caring. Managers who read it that way respond with warnings, performance plans and talks about attitude, which add pressure to a person who is already depleted and usually make things worse. The tell is often the change from baseline. A person who has always been lazy is a different problem from a once-committed person who has started to look lazy, and the second is far more often a sign that something about the work has gone wrong.

It also helps to notice who is most at risk. Burnout often hits the most committed people hardest, because they give the most and find it hardest to stop. The colleague who never says no is more likely to burn out than the one who always does.

It also helps to separate the person from the performance in conversation. "Your reports have had errors" and "you seem exhausted" are both true, and starting with the second makes it far more likely that the first can be solved.

moreFailures.title: Fixing the person instead of the job
moreFailures.body:
It is tempting for organisations to treat burnout as an individual problem, offering resilience training, wellness apps, mindfulness sessions and advice about sleep. These can help a little, and they are not useless. But Maslach and Leiter's research suggests that burnout grows from mismatches between people and their jobs: too much work, too little control, too little recognition, poor teams, unfairness and clashes of values. If those stay the same, the person goes back into the conditions that caused the problem. When you see burnout in someone, ask about the job as well as the person, and change what you can.

When an organisation does change the job, it helps to say so plainly. People who have been offered courses instead of change before may assume the same is happening again, unless they see the workload actually fall.

Wellness offers can also help when they come with time. A mindfulness session in work hours, with cover arranged, sends a different message from an app that people are expected to use in their own time.

A useful test for any wellbeing offer is to ask whether it would still be needed if the job were fixed. If the answer is no, the job is where the effort belongs.

moreFailures.title: Admiring overwork
moreFailures.body:
Many workplaces, and many men, treat long hours, constant availability and working through illness as signs of commitment. The person who answers emails at midnight is praised. The person who leaves on time is quietly judged. This culture rewards exactly the behaviour that leads to burnout, and it makes it harder for people to admit that they are struggling, because struggling looks like weakness. Notice what you praise. Recognising good work rather than long hours, and treating rest and boundaries as normal, makes burnout less likely and easier to talk about.

It also helps to model it yourself. A manager who sends emails at midnight, even with "no need to reply", teaches the team that midnight is when work happens.

Men in particular often measure their worth by how hard they work, and find it difficult to see overwork as a problem until their health or their family forces them to. Praising balance in other men makes it easier for them to choose it.

It also helps to notice the language. "Workhorse", "machine" and "never stops" are often meant as praise, and they describe someone heading for exhaustion.

moreFailures.title: Calling everything burnout
moreFailures.body:
Burnout has become a common word, and it is sometimes used for any kind of tiredness, unhappiness or illness. That can hide other problems. Exhaustion, withdrawal and loss of confidence can come from low mood, anxiety, grief, physical illness, sleep disorders, medication and problems at home. If someone's difficulties reach well beyond work, if they have stopped enjoying anything, if they feel hopeless, or if their health seems affected, the label of burnout may be too narrow. Encourage them to talk to a doctor, and if anything suggests they may be at risk, follow 2.13.

It also helps to remember that burnout and other problems can come together. A man can be burned out by his job and also be depressed, unwell or grieving, and each needs its own response.

It also helps to keep the word in proportion in your own speech. Saying you are burned out after a hard week can make it harder to recognise the real thing, in yourself or in others, when it arrives.

questions.a:
Not in the World Health Organization's classification. ICD-11 lists burn-out as an occupational phenomenon, a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, rather than as a medical condition, and it says the term should refer only to work. Some countries use related diagnoses in their own systems, and doctors may diagnose and treat conditions that overlap with burnout, such as depression, anxiety or sleep disorders. For a reader, the label matters less than the pattern: exhaustion, distance and a falling sense of competence, linked to work, and a change from how the person used to be.

It may also help to know that researchers still debate how burnout relates to depression, and that some people who describe themselves as burned out turn out to be depressed. A doctor can help tell them apart.

It is also worth knowing that the WHO definition is about work, so parents, carers and others outside paid work may find that the word fits their experience without fitting the definition. Researchers have studied similar patterns in those roles.

questions.q: How is burnout different from stress?
questions.a:
Stress is the body's response to demands, and it can be short and even useful: a deadline, a presentation, a busy week. Burnout is what can happen when stress at work goes on for a long time without being managed. It adds two things that ordinary stress usually lacks: a pulling away from the work, often with cynicism, and a fading sense of being any good at it. A stressed person is often still engaged and pushing hard. A burned-out person has often stopped pushing, because the tank is empty and the effort no longer seems worth it.

A quick way to tell the two apart in someone you know is to ask whether they still care. A stressed person usually cares too much. A burned-out person often says they have stopped caring, and is troubled by it.

Burnout also tends to build more slowly than ordinary stress, over months or years, which is why the change from baseline is so often missed by people who see the person every day.

It can help for a while, but it rarely fixes it on its own. Studies of holidays, reviewed by Jessica de Bloom and colleagues, have found that people's health and wellbeing usually improve during a holiday, and that the benefits tend to fade within a few weeks of returning to work. If the work is the same, the burnout tends to come back. Holidays help most when they give real detachment from work, without emails and calls, and when they are combined with changes to the work itself. Regular, smaller breaks, such as evenings and weekends that are genuinely free, may matter as much as the annual holiday.

It also helps to plan the return. The first days back from a holiday are often the most stressful, with a full inbox and a backlog. Keeping the first day light, if possible, can protect some of the benefit.

It also helps to protect the days around a holiday. Working late to clear everything before you go, and working late to catch up when you return, can cancel out much of the rest you had.

questions.q: What can a manager do about it?
questions.a:
More than most managers think. Maslach and Leiter's six areas give a practical checklist. Workload: can anything be removed, delayed or shared? Control: can the person have more say over how and when they work? Reward: is their good work recognised, specifically and often? Community: is the team supportive, and is incivility dealt with? Fairness: are decisions transparent and just? Values: is the person being asked to do things that conflict with what they believe in? A manager who asks about these, and changes what they can, does more for burnout than any number of wellness emails.

It also helps for managers to look after their own load. Managers who are burned out themselves find it hard to notice or help anyone else, and their teams often follow them down.

It also helps to ask the person what would make the biggest difference. People often know exactly which change would help most, and the answer is frequently smaller than managers fear.

It also helps to check in regularly, not just when something goes wrong. A short, routine conversation about workload makes it much easier for someone to say they are struggling before the signs become obvious.

questions.q: What if I am the one burning out?
questions.a:
Start by noticing your own first signs, the earliest changes in your body, behaviour and attitude when work gets out of balance, which the last drill asks you to write down. Protect real rest: evenings, weekends and holidays with genuine detachment from work. Look at the six areas and identify the one or two most out of balance, and raise them with your manager, specifically and calmly. Talk to people outside work. And if your exhaustion, detachment or hopelessness reach beyond work, into the rest of your life, talk to your doctor, because the problem may be more than burnout.

It may also help to talk to someone who has recovered from burnout. Many people find it reassuring to hear that recovery is possible, and useful to hear what changed for them.

It may also help to remember that recovery from burnout often takes months, not weeks, and that the first improvements are often small: sleeping a little better, caring a little more, a joke returning.

It also helps to tell the people close to you what you are noticing. Partners and friends often see the signs before you admit them, and having said it aloud makes it easier to act.

They can help a little, especially when they teach practical skills such as detaching from work, managing sleep and setting boundaries. But they are not a substitute for fixing the job. Burnout grows mainly from mismatches between people and their work, and a course that teaches someone to cope better with an impossible workload leaves the workload in place. Many employees experience resilience training offered in place of real change as a message that the problem is them. The most useful courses are offered alongside changes to workload, control and support, not instead of them.

They can also help managers. Training that teaches managers to spot the signs and to have the conversation is often more useful than training aimed at the people who are already struggling.

It also helps to ask what the people taking the course think of it. If they see it as a substitute for change, it is unlikely to help, however good its content.

watch.title: Why we're burned out and what to do about it, with Christina Maslach
watch.notice: The psychologist who developed the most widely used measure of burnout on its causes. Listen for exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of ineffectiveness, and how each might show in a man's body.
